claim_verdicts.evidence: git show stage-1:scripts/up.sh (tag commit 4fca60a = HEAD): runs `./scripts/dev-secrets.sh`, then `(cd DonHang.App && flutter build web >/dev/null)`, then `docker compose up -d --build --wait`, then echoes "The lab is up." and the site/app/database/lab-box addresses. Order matches claim and Try-it expected result 1.

Dockerfile @ stage-1: `FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:10.0 AS build`, `FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:10.0 AS final`, comment "Npgsql probes for Kerberos/GSSAPI support at startup; without this library present that probe logs a scary but harmless \"cannot open shared object\" line." Npgsql docs: "since Npgsql 10.0 defaults to Prefer, it will attempt to get GSSAPI credentials, and may generate an error such as ... cannot open shared object file" / "falls back ... so the error is harmless." Program.cs runs Database.Migrate() on start, so the connection happens at startup.

docker-compose.yml @ stage-1, service api.environment: `ConnectionStrings__Default: "Host=db;Database=donhang;Username=donhang;Password=${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}"`, `Jwt__SigningKey: "${JWT_SIGNING_KEY}"`. The values themselves come from .env, written by scripts/dev-secrets.sh.

`git grep -i "libgssapi\|gssapi\|krb5" stage-1` hits only DonHang.Api/Dockerfile lines 21 and 23: nothing in the API's code mentions it (verified). But "needed only by the database library" is too strong: .NET docs list libgssapi-krb5-2 among .NET's own Linux dependencies: "if you manually install .NET or you publish a self-contained app, you'll need to make sure these libraries are installed: ... libgssapi-krb5-2".
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: Nothing in the API's code mentions it; the lab installs it because the database library looks for it at startup.

claim_verdicts.evidence: Argument of the lesson restating outline items 1-2 and misconception 2 (track.yaml); not a documented product behaviour, number or syntax. Its over-strong restatement in §4 ("exactly like the first, on any machine, by anyone") is raised separately as an issue.

issues.text: Unlisted claim, contradicted by the repo. scripts/dev-secrets.sh @ stage-1 generates a random JWT key per lab ("random, so every learner's lab has its own, and a token from one machine's api never verifies on another"), and `flutter build web` uses whatever Flutter SDK is on the learner's host (the up.sh comment: "runs on the host, not in a container"). The labs are not the same.
issues.quote: You run the same script every time, and every learner's lab ends up the same.
issues.fix: Replace with: "You run the same script every time, so every learner's lab is built by the same steps." Do not claim identical results.

issues.text: Unconditional promise that contradicts the lesson's own §6 correction ("a script run by hand still depends on who runs it, from which machine, with which files and settings around it") and quiz q4. Writing steps down does not by itself make a deploy identical "on any machine, by anyone".
issues.quote: Then the tenth deploy is done exactly like the first, on any machine, by anyone, and a change to the target is a change to that written list, visible to everyone.
issues.fix: Replace with: "Then the tenth deploy follows the same steps as the first, and a change to the target is a change to that written list, visible to everyone."

issues.text: Outline item 3 not established: "The gap between 'built and tested here' and 'running the same way there' is what the rest of this track — Docker, config, and later CI/CD — closes, one piece at a time." The lesson only points to the next module (Docker); config and the later automated deploy are never named as the remaining pieces. meta.coverage claims item 3 covered.
issues.quote: The next module, Docker, is about how the lab turns that `Dockerfile` into something that runs the same way on every machine.
issues.fix: Add after that sentence: "The rest of this track closes the gap one piece at a time: Docker next, then how the API gets its settings, and in a later stage, deploys run by a program instead of a person." (Avoid the term CI/CD: not in known_vocab ∪ vocab.)

issues.text: Unlisted claim. The tags `sdk:10.0` / `aspnet:10.0` are version tags, not an exact build; .NET docs: including a SHA after the tag "ensures ... that the image is the same as the one you expect". The Dockerfile pins the major.minor version only.
issues.quote: It names the exact .NET 10 build tools used to build the API
issues.fix: Drop "exact": "It names the .NET 10 build tools used to build the API".

issues.text: Unlisted claim, wrong. The previous two lessons are devops.l1.reverse-proxy-basics (does not mention the Dockerfile) and devops.l1.reverse-proxy-and-tls. The Dockerfile was met in devops.l1.what-is-deploy and devops.l1.reverse-proxy-and-tls.
issues.quote: the file you met in the last two lessons
issues.fix: Replace with "the file you met earlier in this module".

issues.text: The GSSAPI probe error is Npgsql-10 behaviour (docs: "since Npgsql 10.0 defaults to Prefer, it will attempt to get GSSAPI credentials"), while versions.yaml pins key npgsql at "9" (samples) and notes the API uses Npgsql 10.0.3 via the EF provider. The lesson names no version and has no claim tied to a version_key; acceptable only because it attributes the behaviour to the Dockerfile comment.
issues.quote: the database library probes for it at startup
issues.fix: Keep the attribution to the comment explicit ("the comment says the database library probes for it at startup") and set claim 2's version_key to efcore (the API's Npgsql comes with the EF Core 10 provider) so an npgsql/efcore bump re-triggers review.

issues.text: Key a is vague and partly unsupported: "only a library needs it" — .NET docs list libgssapi-krb5-2 as a .NET dependency too; the lesson's reason is that nothing in the API's code mentions it and the database library looks for it.
issues.quote: Because only a library needs it, so nobody would remember it
issues.fix: Option a: "Because nothing in the API's code mentions it; the database library looks for it, so a person installs it once and forgets it" (vi accordingly).

issues.text: Explanation c places the signing key in `.env`, but the lesson (§5) says the settings are written down in docker-compose.yml. Both are true in the repo (compose maps ${JWT_SIGNING_KEY} from .env) but the lesson never mentions .env, so the explanation is not grounded in the lesson text.
issues.quote: The signing key is a setting in `.env`; this is a system library.
issues.fix: Explanation c (en): "The signing key is a setting passed in through `docker-compose.yml`; this is a system library." (vi accordingly).

issues.text: SSH is not in known_vocab and is not defined. It opens the situation and labels the first diagram arrow, so I cannot picture what the teammate actually does on the server. The main idea still gets through, so not a blocker.
issues.quote: SSH in, stop the old program, copy the new build over, start it again.
issues.fix: Replace "SSH in" with "log in to the server remotely" in §2, and drop "SSH, " from the diagram arrow label ("stop, copy, start"); or move this lesson after foundation.l1.ssh-and-remote.

issues.text: "connection string" is not in known_vocab and not explained. I can guess it is database-related, but I cannot tell what it contains or why the API needs it.
issues.quote: the connection string and the signing key, arriving as environment variables
issues.fix: Add a few words: "the connection string (where the database is and how to log in to it)".

issues.text: "signing key" is not in known_vocab and not explained. I know JWT, but not that it is signed with a key. The term comes back in quiz q1 (option d explanation) and q5 (option c), so I meet it three times without knowing what it is.
issues.quote: the connection string and the signing key, arriving as environment variables
issues.fix: Add a few words: "the signing key (the secret the API uses to sign and check its JWTs)".

issues.text: §4 and §5 say a written script is the fix and call up.sh "its deploy, written down". Then §6 says a script run by hand still depends on who runs it and from which machine. I run up.sh by hand from my laptop, so I cannot tell whether the lab is an example of the good way or of the second misconception. The step between the two is missing.
issues.quote: You run the same script every time, so every learner's lab is built by the same steps.
issues.fix: Add one sentence after this: up.sh is still run by a person on their own machine, so it fixes the missing steps and the missing target list, but not the problem in the second misconception below. A later stage handles that.

issues.text: In the situation, a missing library stops the API at startup. The lesson's only real example of a missing library, libgssapi-krb5-2, does not stop the API; it only logs a harmless line. I first assumed they were the same library and nearly picked q5 option b ("cannot start at all").
issues.quote: the API stops at startup on a missing library that nobody remembers installing the first time
issues.fix: In §5, add after "never write down": "This one only causes a scary log line; the library in the Friday story was worse, because the API could not start without it."

issues.text: The diagram shows three servers but not what differs between them. Nothing marks S2 as the one that failed, and the prose never walks through the diagram from top to bottom. I had to work out what it contrasts myself.
issues.quote: P2[another person] -->|same steps, from memory| S2[server, two weeks later]
issues.fix: Add one sentence at the start of §4 that walks through the diagram: the first two servers get steps from memory, so the second one can fail; the third gets built from a written definition the same way every time.

issues.text: Step 2 asks me to find the build tools and the runtime in a Dockerfile, but I have never been shown how a Dockerfile is laid out. The comment next to the library makes that part easy. Picking out which lines are the build tools and which are the runtime is guesswork.
issues.quote: list what it says the API needs: which .NET build tools, which runtime, and which extra system library
issues.fix: Add a hint to step 2: "look for the two lines that mention .NET 10; one is the build tools, the other the runtime".

issues.text: The suggested answer quotes an error text, "cannot open shared object", without saying what it means. It is not needed to follow the lesson, but I had to skip it.
issues.quote: logs a frightening "cannot open shared object" line
issues.fix: Add "(the system's way of saying a library file could not be found)" after the quoted error text.

issues.text: I read the closing question twice. It joins two questions with a comma, so it is hard to tell what is being asked.
issues.quote: What went wrong, and it was not the code, so what was it?
issues.fix: Replace with: "The code was not the problem. So what went wrong?"

issues.text: An inline definition sits in the middle of the sentence and pushes "that the API runs on" too far from "runtime". I read it twice.
issues.quote: and the .NET 10 runtime, the part of .NET that runs an already built program, that the API runs on
issues.fix: Split it: "and the .NET 10 runtime that the API runs on. The runtime is the part of .NET that runs an already built program."

issues.text: I can guess the answer from the wording alone. Option c is the longest and the only one that gives a real reason, and option d is obviously silly.
issues.quote: False, because one person still varies the steps, and nobody else can deploy when they are away.
issues.fix: Replace d with a plausible wrong reason of similar length, such as "False, because a senior developer's deploys must always be checked by a second person first."

issues.text: Options b, c and d are clearly impossible (the server writes code, the OS edits scripts, Git hides commits). I can pick a without understanding anything, and a repeats §6 almost word for word.
issues.quote: The script deployed whatever was on that laptop, including uncommitted work
issues.fix: Make one distractor plausible, such as "Someone merged the feature into the main branch after the deploy", so the reader has to use the context (the feature is not on main).

skipped_steps: §5/§6: up.sh is praised as the written deploy, but §6 says a script run by hand still depends on who runs it; the lesson never says which side the lab is on.
§2 vs §5: the Friday library stops the API, libgssapi-krb5-2 does not; the lesson never separates the two.
